newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich to discuss House punishment with public.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich to discuss House punishment with public.

text.p: U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich was due to talk publicly for the first time on Saturday about his unprecedented punishment for ethics violations.

But the embattled Georgia Republican, scheduled to appear at three "town hall" meetings in his home district, planned to keep the discussion about his reprimand and $300,000 fine to a minimum in hopes of avoiding further controversy with opponents in Congress, particularly his Democratic nemesis, U.S. Representative David Bonoir.

The Gingrich staff was preparing to distribute stacks of paper handouts that would outline the speaker's ethics case for hundreds of Georgia residents expected to turn up for the first public forum he has attended at home in weeks.
"It will be very brief. We'll talk about it in a general way, but I'm not going to spend a lot of time on it," Gingrich told Reuters after arriving in Atlanta late Friday from the nation's capital.
"I don't want to get into some game where I say something and then Bonoir or somebody jumps up and says something else," he said.

The 53-year-old conservative and his political allies were struggling to weather a storm of controversy raised by a scathing House ethics committee report and Tuesday's 395-28 vote to reprimand him and impose a $300,000 penalty.

Under an effective plea-bargain arrangement, the committee made no finding as to whether Gingrich used tax-exempt funds illegally for partisan political purposes in the form of his college course, entitled "Renewing American Civilisation." But the former history professor admitted he should have sought legal advice on the question.

The biggest task now before Gingrich was to find a way to pay his six-figure penalty that would not arouse a new furore as the House began a new session. The speaker has been put on notice not to take the money from his campaign warchest.

After returning to Washington from a Republican retreat Thursday, he told reporters that his attorneys were working on a "legal and ethical" solution to the penalty question and promised to make a speech on his punishment "at an appropriate time in the future."

Gingrich's reprimand, and the threat of more controversy from an Internal Revenue Service investigation, has weakened him politically in the House and divided the ranks of his so-called Republican revolution.
But the ethics case has only galvanised his grass-roots support in Georgia and elsewhere in the country.

Despite plans for a protest outside one of his Saturday meeting venues, the speaker's Congressional offices in Washington and Georgia have been flooded this week with calls from supporters, some offering cash donations to help pay for his hefty fine, he said.
